articles.title: The Cellist in the Crater
articles.dek: Paul told a panicked church the time was short and the world was shifting under their feet — then handed them a way to keep living fully anyway.
articles.quote: The crisis around you was never given the authority to divide the devotion inside you.
articles.body:
On May 27, 1992, a mortar shell landed on a bread line in Sarajevo. Twenty-two people, waiting for food in a city under siege, died in seconds. The next day, a cellist named Vedran Smailović put on his formal black tailcoat, carried a plastic chair and his cello into the crater the shell had left, and sat down in the rubble to play. He played Albinoni's Adagio in G minor. He came back the next day, and the next, for twenty-two days straight — one day for each person killed — while snipers in the hills above the city had a clear line of sight to him. Neighbors watched from behind shattered windows, afraid to step outside, and heard something they hadn't expected to hear again: music, unhurried and whole, rising out of a city that was being taken apart piece by piece.

Nobody asked him to do it. It changed nothing about the war. Belgrade did not withdraw its troops because a man played the cello. And yet people who lived through the siege still talk about those twenty-two days as the moment they remembered they were still human beings, not just survivors. Smailović himself later said he wasn't playing to be brave. He was a musician, and a musician plays. The city could burn around him. His hands still had one thing they knew how to do.

Paul is writing to a church that is bracing for its own kind of siege. Corinth, around A.D. 55, is a busy, wealthy, morally loose port city, and the young Christians there have been peppering Paul with anxious questions by letter: Should we marry? Should we stay single? What if we're already engaged — do we call it off? Underneath all of it is a bigger fear. Paul calls it "the present crisis" (1 Corinthians 7:26) — most likely a season of famine, social pressure, and rising hostility toward this new, strange faith. Nobody in Corinth knows exactly what's coming. And in that fog, people are asking Paul to just tell them the rules: marry or don't, so we know how to plan our lives.

Paul refuses to hand them a rulebook. Instead, in verses 25 through 38, he does something more interesting. He says marrying isn't a sin, staying single isn't holier, and anyone who tells you otherwise is adding weight Scripture never asked you to carry (v. 28, 36). What he cares about is something underneath the decision — how a person holds their life, whichever way the decision goes. And he says it in a passage so vivid it reads like he's pulling a curtain back on the whole world at once.

"What I mean, brothers and sisters, is that the time is short. From now on those who have wives should live as if they do not; those who mourn, as if they did not; those who are happy, as if they were not; those who buy something, as if it were not theirs to keep; those who use the things of the world, as if not engrossed in them. For this world in its present form is passing away." (1 Corinthians 7:29–31)

Read quickly, that sounds like Paul telling people to check out — to love their spouse a little less, grieve a little less, celebrate a little less, so nothing hurts too much when it's gone. That's not what he means, and the second half of the passage proves it. A few verses later he says his whole goal is that believers might "live in a right way in undivided devotion to the Lord" (v. 35). Undivided devotion isn't the same as detachment. You can't be devoted to something you've stopped touching.

Here's the turn worth sitting with: Paul isn't asking the Corinthians to love less. He's asking them to stop letting their circumstances be the ones who decide whether they can love, celebrate, grieve, or work at all. "As if not" is not withdrawal — it's freedom from paralysis. The married person keeps loving their spouse, but the marriage isn't what's holding their world together. The grieving person keeps grieving fully, but the grief isn't what gets the final word on who they are. The person who bought a field still tends it, but the field was never going to be the thing that made their life secure. Everything in Corinth was shifting — the food supply, the political weather, the safety of being known as a Christian — and Paul's answer wasn't "detach from your life." It was: don't let the shifting ground stop you from living out loud on top of it.

That's exactly what a man with a cello did in a bombed square in Sarajevo. He didn't pretend the siege wasn't happening. He didn't need the shelling to stop before he could play beautifully. He carried his one undivided thing — his devotion to the music he knew how to make — straight into the middle of the crisis, and let it be full-strength there. The crater didn't get to decide whether the Adagio would be worth playing. He decided.

You don't need a siege to feel this. Maybe it's a flooded street outside your window this week, the rain still falling harder than the forecast promised, or a paycheck that isn't stretching the way it used to, or a diagnosis you're still getting used to saying out loud. Paul isn't offering you an escape hatch from any of that. He's pointing at something sturdier than an escape hatch: the thing you were devoted to before the crisis started doesn't have to wait for the crisis to end. You can keep loving the people in your house tonight. You can keep showing up honestly to your grief, your joy, your ordinary Tuesday responsibilities — not because the ground has stopped moving, but because none of those things were ever standing on the ground in the first place. They were standing on him.

This is, in its own quiet way, a very Filipino instinct already. It's the instinct behind cooking a full meal for guests during a blackout, candles and all. It's the instinct behind still showing up to a cousin's wedding after the flight got rebooked twice because of the weather. Filipinos already know how to keep living fully in the middle of an inconvenient sky. Paul is simply naming the reason why that instinct is right, and pointing it toward something larger than good manners: a devotion to Christ so undivided that no crisis, however loud, gets to decide whether it still counts.

So here is one thing to carry out of this passage today, the way Vedran Smailović carried a chair into a crater: pick the one act of devotion the crisis in your life is currently tempting you to postpone. A phone call. A prayer you've been meaning to actually finish instead of starting. A kindness you've been saving for calmer weather. Do it today, in full, right in the middle of things. Not because the weather will improve if you do. Because it was never the weather's decision to make.

articles.title: The Ring That Had to Go Through Fire
articles.dek: Job couldn't find God anywhere he looked — so why did he say he'd come out like gold?
articles.quote: He knows the way that I take; when he has tested me, I will come forth as gold.
articles.body:
On Ongpin Street in the heart of Manila's old Chinatown, a young woman named Divine once carried her lola's wedding ring into a cramped little goldsmith's stall, her hands shaking. Two pawnshops had already turned it away that same morning, telling her it was probably tumbaga, a gold-colored alloy mostly made of copper, worth almost nothing. It was the only thing she had left of her grandmother, and she needed to know the truth, even if the truth hurt. The old goldsmith didn't argue with her or with the pawnshops. He scratched the ring across a small black touchstone, dripped acid onto the streak, and watched the color. Then, before she could stop him, he held the ring itself over an open flame until it glowed orange. Divine flinched, sure he was ruining the one heirloom she had. "Totoong ginto," he said calmly, turning it in the light once it cooled. Real gold. It doesn't melt away in fire. It only comes out brighter. The ring survived. What made it precious wasn't that it looked golden under a store light. It was that it could pass through the one test every fake fails.

Centuries before any goldsmith tested a ring this way, a suffering man named Job was going through something strikingly similar, except he was the one being tested, and he could not find the one doing the testing. By the time we reach Job 23, Job has lost his children, his wealth, his health, and now even the comfort of his friends, who keep insisting his suffering must be punishment for some hidden sin. Job answers them by saying, in effect: if I could only find God, I could state my case and be done with this. "If only I knew where to find him; if only I could go to his dwelling!" he says (Job 23:3). He imagines standing before God's own bench, confident he would be cleared: "I would find out what he would answer me, and consider what he would say" (Job 23:5). But God will not be located. "If I go to the east, he is not there; if I go to the west, I do not find him. When he is at work in the north, I do not see him; when he turns to the south, I catch no glimpse of him" (Job 23:8-9). Job searches all four directions and comes home with nothing. And then, right in the middle of that failed search, he says something that stops you cold.

"But he knows the way that I take; when he has tested me, I will come forth as gold." (Job 23:10, NIV)

Notice what Job does not say. He doesn't say he finally found God, or finally understood why this happened to him. He never gets an explanation. In fact, the very next chapter is Job listing every unresolved injustice he can think of: the poor going hungry in the cold, the fatherless orphan whose ox is led away, the wicked who seem to get away with everything while "God charges no one with wrongdoing" (Job 24:12). Job never resolves that tension. What he has instead is one stubborn conviction: he knows the way that I take. That word "way" means the actual road, the specific path Job is walking on this particular day, with all its particular pain. Job cannot see God. But he trusts that God sees him. It's worth sitting with why that distinction matters so much, because it means the goldsmith doesn't need to be visible to the ring for the testing to be real, fair, or purposeful. A ring in the flame doesn't feel the intention behind the heat. It only feels the heat. Faith, for Job, was never certainty about outcomes. It was confidence in the character of the one holding the flame, sight unseen.

That confidence gets tested again almost immediately. Bildad, one of Job's three friends, offers his shortest and coldest speech in the whole book, just six verses reminding Job how small and impure any human being is compared to God: "How then can a mortal be righteous before God? How can one born of woman be pure? If even the moon is not bright and the stars are not pure in his eyes, how much less a mortal, who is but a maggot" (Job 25:4-6). It's technically true, and it answers absolutely nothing. Job's reply, though, is remarkable. Instead of arguing back or collapsing, he lifts his eyes to creation itself and marvels at what God has already, quietly, done: he "spreads out the northern skies over empty space; he suspends the earth over nothing" (Job 26:7). Long before anyone owned a telescope or understood gravity, Job noticed that the earth simply hangs there, held up by nothing anyone can see or touch, and somehow it never falls. That's the same lesson as the flame, dressed differently. The earth doesn't need visible pillars to stay steady. Job doesn't need a visible God to stay steady either. Something unseen is doing the holding in both cases, and it can be trusted precisely because it has always, without fail, been trustworthy.

Maybe you know exactly what it feels like to search every direction and come up empty: praying over a diagnosis, a child who's drifted, a marriage under strain, a job that fell through at the last minute, and hearing nothing back. Job gives you permission to say that plainly, without pretending it doesn't hurt. Chapter 24 is proof that even a man of deep faith is allowed to ask hard, unresolved questions about suffering and injustice. But Job also hands you something to actually hold onto inside that silence: not an explanation, but a trust that the one testing you already knows precisely which road you're walking, and precisely how much heat real gold can take before it would ever be ruined. He has never once miscalculated a temperature. He never will.

The next time you feel like you've searched for God in every direction and found nothing, at your desk, in a waiting room, in a quiet house at two in the morning, try borrowing Job's line instead of demanding an answer you may not get today. Say it slowly, the way Divine's goldsmith turned that ring in the light: he knows the way that I take. You don't have to locate God to be held by him. You only have to let the fire do what fire has always done to real gold, and trust that what comes out the other side will be worth everything it cost to get there.

articles.title: Before the World Wakes Up
articles.dek: A scientist born into slavery kept a strange daily habit no one asked him to keep — and it turned out to be the whole secret of his joy.
articles.quote: The wise don't wait to feel grateful. They show up for it at the same two hours every day, and let the feeling catch up.
articles.body:
Long before sunrise, while the rest of Tuskegee Institute was still asleep, George Washington Carver would slip out of his room with a lantern and walk into the woods alone. He did this almost every morning of his adult life. He called it going to his "little workshop" with God. He wasn't praying for anything in particular. He was simply showing up — to look at a leaf, a weed, a plant nobody else thought was worth a second glance — and to thank the God who made it before he let the day's demands get their hands on him.

Carver had been born enslaved in Missouri, kidnapped as an infant along with his mother by raiders, and returned — alone — by the man who'd once owned him, in exchange for a horse. He was orphaned, sickly, turned away from colleges for the color of his skin, and would spend his whole career in a country that didn't fully believe he deserved credit for what he discovered. And yet visitors to Tuskegee kept remarking on the same strange thing: the man was glad. Not performatively cheerful — quietly, steadily glad, in a way that didn't seem to depend on how the world was treating him that week. When they asked him why, he pointed to those early mornings. "Everything is possible for the man who believes," he'd say, but what he practiced was smaller than belief. It was a habit. He met God before sunrise, and he met God again before he slept. Everything else in his day was built on those two appointments.

That habit is almost exactly what Psalm 92 is describing — and it's easy to walk past this psalm without noticing how specific it actually is. The heading tells us it was written for the Sabbath, one day set apart to say out loud what's supposed to be true every day, so it doesn't get lost in the noise of the other six. And the psalm doesn't open with a request. It opens with an instruction to itself: it is good to do this. Not "it feels good when I'm in the mood." Good — the way rain is good for a field, whether the field feels like receiving it or not.

Then the psalmist gets specific about timing, and this is the detail worth slowing down on:

It is good to praise the LORD and make music to your name, O Most High, proclaiming your love in the morning and your faithfulness at night. (Psalm 92:1-2, NIV)

Morning and night. Not "whenever I remember" — the two bookends of the day, on purpose, every day. Here's what's easy to miss: those two words are doing different work. In the morning, you praise God's love — before you've earned anything, before the day has proven itself, on pure trust that today will hold what love holds. At night, you praise his faithfulness — now that the day is done and you can look back and see, item by item, that he actually came through. Morning praise takes courage, because nothing's been confirmed yet. Night praise takes honesty, because you have to actually look back and notice. The psalmist isn't leaving this to chance or mood. He's building a rhythm sturdy enough to hold both kinds of days — the ones that go well and the ones that don't.

And then, a few verses later, comes the reason this rhythm is worth keeping at all: "For you make me glad by your deeds, LORD; I sing for joy at the works of your hands. How great are your works, LORD, how profound your thoughts!" (Psalm 92:4-5). The gladness isn't self-generated. It's a response to something he keeps noticing — the actual, specific works of God's hands. That's exactly what Carver was doing in the woods at 4 a.m. He wasn't manufacturing gratitude out of nothing. He was going looking for the works of God's hands in a peanut plant, and finding them, morning after morning, until noticing became instinct.

Here's the part of Psalm 92 that gives the whole thing its edge, though. Right after the psalmist describes his own gladness, he turns and names the people who don't have it: "Senseless people do not know, fools do not understand, that though the wicked spring up like grass and all evildoers flourish, they will be destroyed forever" (Psalm 92:6-7). It's worth asking why that line sits right here, in the middle of a psalm about morning and evening praise. The answer seems to be this: the fool's mistake isn't wickedness so much as short attention. He looks at grass springing up fast and green and mistakes speed for permanence. He never developed the habit of looking twice, of noticing what actually lasts versus what only looks good this week. The wise person in this psalm isn't smarter. He's just been paying closer attention, morning and night, for longer.

That's freeing news for anyone who assumes gratitude is a personality trait some people were simply issued at birth and others weren't. Carver wasn't a naturally sunny man handed an easy life. He built the gladness the same way you'd build any strength — with repetition, at a fixed hour, whether or not he felt like it that day. The habit came first. The feeling followed, most days, but not because he waited for it to show up on its own.

You don't need a lantern or a forest to try this. You need two fixed moments — one before the day gets its hooks in you, one after it's done — and a short, specific question at each: what did his hands make today, and where was his love already ahead of me before I woke up? Some mornings the honest answer will be small. That's fine. Carver spent years studying a single plant before anyone called it useful. Smallness noticed consistently is exactly what this psalm is asking for.

Try it for one week. Before you check your phone tomorrow morning, name one thing that's still true and good regardless of how the day goes. Before you sleep tomorrow night, name one thing God actually did, not just one thing you hoped he'd do. That's the whole practice. It isn't dramatic. It wasn't dramatic for Carver either — just a lantern, a path he'd walked a thousand times, and a willingness to keep showing up before anyone else was awake to see it.

articles.title: The Crown That Wasn't Gold
articles.dek: Folly doesn't build her own house. She copies Wisdom's — same street, same seat, same opening line — and hopes you never ask what's underneath.
articles.quote: Folly is not a rival house across town, clearly marked with warning signs. She is a forgery, engineered to be mistaken for the real thing.
articles.body:
In 250 BC, King Hiero II of Syracuse handed a goldsmith a bar of pure gold and commissioned a crown fit for the gods, a votive offering meant to hang in a temple as thanks for his throne. When it came back, the crown gleamed exactly the way gold should gleam. It weighed exactly what the gold bar had weighed. By every visible measure, it was flawless, the kind of object a king could proudly display for the rest of his reign. But a rumor reached Hiero anyway: the goldsmith had skimmed off some of the gold for himself and quietly alloyed in silver to make up the missing weight. The crown looked right. It felt right in the hand. It passed every test a person could run with their eyes and their fingers. And there was no way, just by looking at it, to prove it wasn't real.

Hiero handed the puzzle to a mathematician named Archimedes, who is said to have still been turning it over in his mind when he lowered himself into a public bath and watched the water rise around him. He realized that an object's true substance could be measured not by its shape or its shine, but by what it displaced. Legend has it he leapt out and ran through the streets of Syracuse shouting "Eureka!" — "I have found it!" — because he'd discovered a way to catch a fraud that was invisible to the naked eye. You could not tell a counterfeit crown from a genuine one by looking. You could only tell by testing what was underneath.

Proverbs 9 ends with a crown just like that one.

The chapter opens with a woman named Wisdom, building a fine house and setting a fine table. "She has sent out her servants, and she calls from the highest point of the city, 'Let all who are simple come to my house!' To those who lack judgment, she says, 'Come, eat my food and drink the wine I have mixed. Leave your simple ways and you will live; walk in the way of insight'" (Prov 9:3–6). It's a real invitation to a real feast, generous and life-giving.

Then, in the chapter's closing verses, a second woman shows up — and she is unsettlingly familiar. "Folly is an unruly woman; she is simple and knows nothing" (Prov 9:13). Watch where she sets up: "She sits at the door of her house, on a seat at the highest point of the city, calling out to those who pass by" (Prov 9:14–15) — the exact address Wisdom just used. And then listen to her opening line: "'Let all who are simple come to my house!' And to those who lack judgment she says" (Prov 9:16). Read that again next to verse 4. It is not a similar sentence. In the Hebrew and in our English translations, it is the identical sentence, word for word.

Folly didn't write her own material. She copied Wisdom's address, borrowed her seat, and recited her opening line back, unchanged. Only then does she add her own pitch:

"Stolen water is sweet; food eaten in secret is delicious!" But little do they know that the dead are there, that her guests are deep in the realm of the dead. (Prov 9:17–18)

Here's the insight worth sitting with: Folly is not a rival house across town, clearly marked with warning signs. She is a forgery, engineered to be mistaken for the real thing. Same corner. Same welcome. Same words, right down to the syllable. The only place she can't fake it is underneath — in what's actually being served once the door closes behind you. Wisdom's table has bread, wine, and a future. Folly's table has secrecy dressed up as sweetness, and a grave underneath the floorboards.

This is deeply practical, because most of us were never taught to test what's inside — only to notice how something looks from the road. We assume that if an invitation sounds generous, feels exciting, or even uses the right words, it must be trustworthy. But a scam text now looks exactly like a message from your bank, down to the logo and the font. A counterfeit bill passes every glance and every fold. And the choices that quietly wreck a marriage, a conscience, or a career rarely arrive looking dangerous — they arrive looking like an upgrade on something good, whispered with the promise that no one has to know, wearing the same friendly voice as everything that's actually kept you safe.

Think of the last time someone said, "It's fine, walang malalaman" — about padding a report, about a friendship that was growing in a direction it shouldn't, about looking away because everyone else was doing it too. Every one of those moments is Folly, sitting at the very corner Wisdom sits on, using nearly her exact words: come in, it's simple, you lack nothing here. The tell was never in her tone of voice. It was always in what she was hiding under the floor.

That's her oldest and best line: stolen water is sweet. Not because sin is actually superior, but because secrecy makes an ordinary thing feel forbidden, and forbidden feels thrilling. The sweetness is real, for a moment — the same way a counterfeit coin really does shine, and really does spend, right up until someone finally weighs it. But Proverbs insists you were never meant to judge the water by its shine or its taste in the first ten seconds. You were meant to ask where you'll be standing once you've swallowed it, once the secret has done what secrets do and settled into the foundation of your life.

This is where the gospel does something Archimedes' bathtub never could. Testing a crown only proves it's fake — it can't turn silver back into gold. But Jesus doesn't just expose the counterfeit and leave you holding a worthless coin. He offers a trade: your folly for his wisdom, freely, at his own table. "Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28) is Wisdom's invitation, finally spoken by someone you can trust completely — because he went down into the grave Folly only pretends to hide, and walked back out the other side. He is the one guest who left that house alive, and now he holds the door open for anyone who wants to follow him out.

So here's something to actually do today. Before you walk through any door — a shortcut, a secret, a compromise wearing the costume of freedom — run the one test that matters. Not "does this look and sound good," but "if I follow this all the way down, where do I end up?" Wisdom's house and Folly's house can look identical from the road. But you've been handed a Word that tells you exactly what's cooking behind each one. Use it before you knock, not after you're already sitting at the table.
